## Proof

We evaluate $\int_{[0,1]} g\,d\mu$ where $d\mu$ is Lebesgue (Borel) measure and
$$g(x)=\begin{cases}1,&x\in C\\ x,&x\in[0,1]\setminus C.\end{cases}$$

**Key fact.** The Cantor set $C$ has Lebesgue measure $\mu(C)=0$. (It is constructed by removing intervals of total length $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}2^{n-1}/3^{n}=1$, so the remaining set has measure $1-1=0$.)

Since $C$ and $[0,1]\setminus C$ are disjoint measurable sets whose union is $[0,1]$, by additivity of the Lebesgue integral over disjoint measurable sets,
$$\int_{[0,1]} g\,d\mu=\int_{C} g\,d\mu+\int_{[0,1]\setminus C} g\,d\mu.$$

**First term.** On $C$, $g\equiv 1$. Since $\mu(C)=0$,
$$\int_{C} g\,d\mu=\int_{C}1\,d\mu=\mu(C)=0.$$

**Second term.** On $[0,1]\setminus C$, $g(x)=x$. The function $h(x)=x$ is measurable and integrable on $[0,1]$. Since $C$ has measure zero, modifying a function on a null set does not change its Lebesgue integral. Therefore
$$\int_{[0,1]\setminus C} g\,d\mu=\int_{[0,1]\setminus C} x\,d\mu=\int_{[0,1]} x\,d\mu.$$

Computing the last integral (Riemann = Lebesgue for continuous functions on a compact interval):
$$\int_{[0,1]} x\,d\mu=\int_{0}^{1}x\,dx=\frac{x^{2}}{2}\Big|_{0}^{1}=\frac{1}{2}.$$

**Combining.**
$$\int_{[0,1]} g\,d\mu=0+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{2}.$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
